title: Conditional expert handshake profiling & mismatch notes
summary: Working notes on a recurring p99 latency pattern tied to conditional expert 'handshakes' in MoE routes. Cross-arch differences (Llama/Mistral/Qwen) observed for long context loads. Contains traces, hypotheses, and an experiment matrix to reproduce/mitigate.
content:
Purpose and scope:
- Document a weird, reproducible p99 tail that manifests when the router takes conditional (non-deterministic) expert choices during long-context decodes (~4k+ tokens).
- Compare behavior across three model families (Llama-derived, Mistral-derived, Qwen-derived MoE variants).
- Focus on the handshake between the routing layer and expert execution: enqueue/ack, KV cache warmup, per-expert queue flush, and cross-device scatter/gather.

High-level observed symptom:
- For mixed-batch loads with variable sequence lengths we see occasional 30–120ms spikes at the per-request level on top of baseline 40ms p50 for 2k token windows.
- Spikes correlate with (a) a high fraction of requests that trigger experts on a different GPU, and (b) sequences that cross the 'large-kv' threshold in our runtime (past ~2048 tokens) where we switch tile layout.
- Llama-variant shows fewer spikes overall; Mistral and Qwen variants show higher variance and a second-mode p99 at ~180ms in worst cases.

Initial hypotheses (ordered by likelihood):
1) Handshake delay on remote-expert enqueue: asynchronous queue depth + backpressure can cause variable wait for acknowledgement before the route continues.
2) KV cache format switch triggers extra memcpy and kernel rebinds that block the router-to-expert handoff in some hardware/arch combos.
3) Routing softmax vs top-k gating implementation differences cause different expert fanout sizes, leading to serialization overhead in the scatter/gather path.
4) Per-expert kernel launch jitter due to non-coalesced launches (more prominent on Ampere+, less on older Turing).

Reproduction recipe (minimal):
- Use dedicated test-cluster (d-2g-persist) with two GPUs and long-context preset: --seq-len 4096, --batch 8 variable-length (1..4096).
- Model: {variant} MoE 24B, 16 experts, router threshold tuned to 0.3.
- Workload: mixture of short chitchat and long-doc summarization to force hot/cold expert switching.
- Tooling: enable trace logging (ROUTER_TRACE=1), nvtx markers, per-kernel timestamps, and runtime sampling (1% of requests) to capture full cross-device call stacks.

Quick trace excerpt (annotated):
- [0001] recv-request (0ms) -> tokenize (3ms) -> route-decision (6ms) -> enqueue-expert-A (6ms)
- [0001] enqueue-expert-A (6ms) -> ack (6ms) [fast path when expert local]
- [0042] enqueue-expert-B (local false) (12ms) -> remote-queue-post (45ms) -> wait-for-ack (87ms) -> continue (88ms) => big tail
- nvprof snapshot shows long host->device memcpy preceding expert kernel on remote GPU when context > 2048 tokens.

Cross-arch notes (empirical):
- Llama-derived MoE: routing output tends to be more concentrated (smaller fanout) in our traces; fewer disk/GPU hops observed. Lower p99. Possibly gating implementation favors sharper logits.
- Mistral-derived MoE: gating outputs broader expert selections for same threshold; leads to more cross-device traffic and higher probability of enqueuing remote experts. p99 increased.
- Qwen-derived MoE: intermediate fanout but more frequent KV format switches; runtime path triggers extra memcpy when the sequence length crosses 2048 boundary (we suspect layout decisions in the exported ONNX/torchscript).

Profiling artifacts and metrics captured:
- per-request timeline traces (ROUTER_TRACE) — stored by request id (sampled 1%).
- kernel launch timing matrix: kernel_name -> avg_ms, p50, p95, p99.
- host->device copy sizes: distribution around handshake points.
- expert-queue depth histograms and dequeue latency CDFs.

Experiment matrix (planned):
1) Force-local-expert mode: route all experts to same node (simulate scheduler affinity) -> measure p99. If tail disappears, root cause=remote enqueue/backpressure.
2) Disable KV-layout-switch (pin to small-kv layout) -> measure p99. If tail reduces, root cause=memcpy+layout rebind.
3) Replace softmax gating with top-k gating (at router) in runtime stubbing -> measure fanout and p99.
4) Pre-touch remote expert memory (keep allocated persistent buffers) to avoid on-demand cudaMalloc/copies -> measure kernel startup jitter.

Preliminary results (short summary):
- Experiment 1 (force-local): p99 drops ~50% for Mistral/Qwen variants. Llama shows small improvement (~10%). Suggests remote-enqueue/backpressure is big factor for Mistral/Qwen.
- Experiment 2 (disable layout switch): p99 improved modestly for Qwen, negligible for Mistral/Llama. Qwen's exported runtime path likely triggers extra copies during layout migration.
- Experiment 3 (top-k gating): fanout decreased by ~18% for Mistral, p99 improved by ~12ms on average. Suggests gating soft implementation contributes.

Micro-optimizations attempted (notes):
- Batched remote enqueues: group many small enqueues into a single RPC to remote worker. Reduced host->device roundtrips but increased jitter for short sequences (unfavorable to low-latency short requests).
- Async memcpy pipeline (pre-copy predicted large-KV segments based on token prefix): reduced remote kernel stall by ~20ms on Qwen testcases. Prediction heuristics brittle.
- Per-expert dedicated worker threads kept pinned to avoid kernel launch jitter; reduced p99 spikes by ~8–15ms consistently.

Open questions / TODOs:
- Why does Mistral gating produce broader fanout for identical routing weight distribution? Possibilities: model export differences (softmax temperature applied), numerical differences in float16 stability, or tokenization differences causing different per-token statistics. Need to inspect gating logits distribution side-by-side.
- Are there hidden allocator calls (cudaMalloc) on Qwen path tied to ONNX runtime that we aren't accounting for? Need to run cuda-memcheck/allocator trace on the worst-case reproduction.
- Router->executor handshake protocol: current ack semantics block the request until ack received. Could switch to speculative decoding where we optimistically proceed and reconcile later — tradeoff complexity vs correctness/consistency. Prototype simulation required.

Action items (owners):
- Marcus: run allocator traces for Qwen on d-2g-persist, capture cudaMalloc/cudaFree timestamps (due 2025-10-06).
- Aisha: instrument gating logits export for all three variants and produce side-by-side histograms (due 2025-09-25).
- Lena: prototype 'speculative-continue' simulation in runtime (feature branch) to test whether early continuation reduces p99 without causing incorrect outputs (due 2025-10-09).
- Tomás: evaluate RPC batching heuristics and document tradeoffs (due 2025-10-02).

Notes on longer-term mitigations:
- Scheduler affinity hints: prefer collocating frequently co-invoked experts to reduce cross-device hops. Requires workload-aware placement and possibly online hotset detection in router.
- Adaptive gating calibration: automatically tune gating temperature / top-k to respect a target expected fanout under latency SLOs.
- Persistent per-expert memory pools allocated at model load time to avoid on-demand device-side allocations.

Related tickets and references:
- RED-2417: "p99 spikes for long-context MoE routes" (investigation ticket)
- PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/879 (initial speculative-continue prototype)
- Confluence draft: perf/handshake-mismatch (link above)

Free-form notes / scratch (things I tried interactively):
- run: ./tools/run_bench --model qwen-moe-24b --seq 4096 --batch 8 --sampled-trace 1%
- nvprof: noticed host->device memcpy of ~12MB right before expert kernel when seq>2048, no such copy for Llama builds.
- manual kernel timeline looked like: host->copy -> host wait -> cudastream sync -> kernel launch -> kernel wait -> return. Trying to remove the host wait by using CUDA events + non-blocking streams.

Conclusion (current working hypothesis):
- The p99 tail is multi-factorial but heavily influenced by remote-expert enqueue/ack delays and arch/export-specific KV layout switching. Mistral's gating behaviour increases the chance of remote hops; Qwen's runtime path triggers extra memory operations at long contexts.
- Short-term mitigations: scheduler affinity + persistent expert pools + gating calibration. Longer-term: rethink handshake semantics (speculative continuation) and improve model export parity.

Please add experimental notes below when you run reproductions (sampled traces are key).

-- Marcus
